modern:
The bride wants to give Jesus everything she produces. Our heart has “all manner of pleasant fruits,” both “old and new,” and they are laid up for our Beloved. At this rich autumn season of fruit, let’s look over what we have stored. We have *new* fruits. We want to feel new life, new joy, new gratitude; we want to make new resolutions and carry them out with new work; our heart blossoms with new prayers, and our soul is pledging herself to new efforts. But we have some *old* fruits too. There is our first love: a choice fruit, that one! And Jesus delights in it. There is our first faith: that simple faith by which, having nothing, we came to possess all things. There is our joy when we first knew the Lord: let’s bring it back to life. We have our old memories of the promises. How faithful God has been! In sickness, how softly he made our bed! In deep waters, how calmly he held us up! In the flaming furnace, how graciously he rescued us! Old fruits, indeed! We have many of them, for his mercies have been more than the hairs of our head. We must regret old sins, but then we have had the repentances he has given us, by which we have wept our way to the cross and learned the worth of his blood.

We have fruits this morning, both new and old; but here is the point: *they are all laid up for Jesus*. Truly, the best and most acceptable service is the kind in which Jesus is the soul’s only aim, and his glory, with nothing else mixed in at all, is the goal of all our efforts. Let our many fruits be laid up only for our Beloved; let’s bring them out when he is with us, and not hold them up for people to stare at. Jesus, we’ll turn the key in our garden door, and no one will come in to rob you of one good fruit from the soil you have watered with your bloody sweat. Our all will be yours, yours only, O Jesus, our Beloved!

modern: Jehovah is generous by nature; giving is his delight. His gifts are precious beyond measure, and are given as freely as the light of the sun. He gives grace to his elect because he wills it, to his redeemed because of his covenant, to the called because of his promise, to believers because they seek it, to sinners because they need it. He gives grace abundantly, at the right time, constantly, readily, sovereignly, doubling the value of the gift by the way he gives it. Grace in all its forms he freely gives to his people: comforting, preserving, sanctifying, directing, instructing, helping grace he pours generously into their souls without ceasing, and he always will, whatever may happen. Sickness may come, but the Lord will give grace; poverty may happen to us, but grace will surely be given; death must come, but grace will light a candle at the darkest hour. Reader, how blessed it is, as the years roll round and the leaves begin to fall again, to enjoy such an unfading promise as this: “The Lord will give grace.”

The little word “*and*” in this verse is a diamond rivet joining the present to the future: grace and glory always go together. God has married them, and no one can divorce them. The Lord will never deny glory to a soul he has freely allowed to live on his grace. In fact, glory is nothing more than grace in its Sunday best, grace in full bloom, grace like autumn fruit, mellow and ripened. How soon we may have glory, no one can tell! It may be that before this month of October has run out, we’ll see the Holy City; but whether the wait is longer or shorter, we’ll be glorified before long. Glory, the glory of heaven, the glory of eternity, the glory of Jesus, the glory of the Father: the Lord will surely give it to his chosen. Oh, what a rare promise from a faithful God!

modern:
Our hope in Christ for the future is the mainspring and the mainstay of our joy here. It will lift our hearts to think often about heaven, for everything we could want is promised there. Here we are weary and worn out with work, but over there is the land of *rest*, where the sweat of labor will no longer wet the worker’s forehead, and tiredness will be banished forever. To those who are weary and spent, the word “rest” is full of heaven. We’re always on the battlefield; we are so tempted within, and so harassed by enemies without, that we have little or no peace. But in heaven we’ll enjoy the *victory*, when the banner will be waved high in triumph and the sword put back in its sheath, and we’ll hear our Captain say, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” We have suffered one loss after another, but we are going to the land of the *immortal*, where graves are unknown. Here sin is a constant grief to us, but there we’ll be perfectly *holy*, for nothing that defiles will ever enter that kingdom. Hemlock doesn’t spring up in the furrows of heaven’s fields. Oh, isn’t it a joy that you won’t be in exile forever, that you won’t live forever in this wilderness, but will soon inherit Canaan?

Still, let it never be said of us that we’re dreaming about the *future* and forgetting the *present*. Let the future make the present holy and put it to the highest uses. Through the Spirit of God, the hope of heaven is the most powerful force there is for producing goodness. It is a fountain of joyful effort; it is the cornerstone of cheerful holiness. The person who has this hope goes about his work with energy, for the joy of the Lord is his strength. He fights temptation with passion, for the hope of the next world drives back the fiery darts of the enemy. He can work without reward now, for he looks for a reward in the world to come.

modern:
Child of God, do you hesitate to claim this title for yourself? Ah, has your unbelief made you forget that you too are “greatly beloved”? Mustn’t you have been greatly loved, to have been bought with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot? When God struck his only Son for you, what was that but being greatly loved? You lived in sin and ran wild in it: mustn’t you have been greatly loved for God to have put up with you so patiently? You were called by grace and led to a Savior, and made a child of God and an heir of heaven. All this proves, doesn’t it, a very great and overflowing love? Since then, whether your path has been rough with troubles or smooth with mercies, it has been full of proofs that you are “a man greatly beloved.” If the Lord has disciplined you, it wasn’t in anger; if he has made you poor, in grace you have been rich. The more unworthy you feel, the more evidence you have that nothing but love beyond words could have led the Lord Jesus to save a soul like yours. The more you feel how little you deserve, the more clearly God’s overflowing love shows in choosing you, calling you and making you an heir of bliss.

Now, if there is such love between God and us, let’s live under its influence and sweetness, and use the privileges of our position. Let’s not come to our Lord as if we were strangers, or as if he were unwilling to hear us, for we are greatly loved by our loving Father. “He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” Come boldly, believer, for in spite of Satan’s whispers and your own heart’s doubts, you are greatly loved. Think this evening about how great and faithful God’s love is, and so go to bed in peace.

modern: Angels are the unseen attendants of God’s people; they carry us in their hands so that we don’t strike our foot against a stone. Loyalty to their Lord makes them take a deep interest in the children of his love. They rejoice when the prodigal comes back to his father’s house below, and they welcome the believer’s arrival at the King’s palace above. In olden times the sons of God were favored with seeing them, and today, although we don’t see them, heaven is still open, and the angels of God go up and come down on the Son of Man, so that they may visit the heirs of salvation. Seraphim still fly with live coals from the altar to touch the lips of people greatly loved. If our eyes could be opened, we’d see horses of fire and chariots of fire around the Lord’s servants; for we have come to an innumerable company of angels, who all watch over and protect the royal family. Spenser’s line is no poetic make-believe, where he sings:

What dignity the chosen are raised to, when heaven’s brilliant courtiers become their willing servants! What fellowship we’re raised to, since we have dealings with spotless heavenly beings! How well we are defended, since all the twenty thousand chariots of God are armed to rescue us! Who do we owe all this to? Let the Lord Jesus Christ be dear to us forever, for through him we are made to sit in heavenly places, far above principalities and powers. He is the one whose camp is around those who fear him; he is the true Michael, whose foot is on the dragon. All hail, Jesus! You Angel of Jehovah’s presence, to you this family offers its morning vows.

modern:
It’s an ordinary thought, and yet it tastes like nectar to the weary heart: Jesus was tempted as I am. You have heard that truth many times; have you grasped it? He was tempted to the very same sins we fall into. Don’t separate Jesus from our shared humanity. It’s a dark room you’re going through, but Jesus went through it first. It’s a sharp fight you’re in, but Jesus has stood toe to toe with the same enemy. Let’s cheer up: Christ has carried the load before us, and the bloodstained footprints of the King of glory can be seen along the road we are walking right now.

There’s something sweeter still: Jesus was tempted, but Jesus never sinned. Then, my soul, you don’t have to sin, for Jesus was a man, and if one man endured these temptations and didn’t sin, then in his power his members may also stop sinning. Some beginners in the Christian life think they can’t be tempted without sinning, but they’re mistaken. There is no sin in *being tempted*, but there *is* sin in *giving in to temptation*. Here is comfort for those who are badly tempted. There is still more to encourage them, if they remember that the Lord Jesus, though tempted, gloriously triumphed. And as he overcame, so surely will his followers, for Jesus stands for his people as their representative; the Head has triumphed, and the members share in the victory.

Our fears are needless, for Christ is with us, armed to defend us. Our place of safety is in the Savior’s arms. Perhaps we are being tempted right now to drive us closer to him. Blessed be any wind that blows us into the harbor of our Savior’s love! Happy wounds, which make us look for the beloved Physician! You who are tempted, come to your tempted Savior, for he can be touched with the feeling of your weaknesses, and he will help every tried and tempted one.

modern: We often look ahead with dread to *old age*, forgetting that in the evening it will be light. For many saints, old age is the best season of their lives. A gentler breeze cools the sailor’s cheek as he nears the shore of immortality; fewer waves ruffle his sea; quiet reigns, deep, still and solemn. The flashes of youth’s fire are gone from the altar of age, but the truer flame of earnest feeling remains. The pilgrims have reached the land of Beulah, that happy country whose days are like the days of heaven on earth. Angels visit it, heavenly breezes blow over it, flowers of paradise grow in it, and the air is full of angelic music. Some live here for years, and others reach it only a few hours before they depart, but it is an Eden on earth. We may well long for the time when we’ll rest in its shady groves and be satisfied with hope until the time comes for it to be fulfilled. The setting sun looks larger than when it’s high in the sky, and a splendor of glory colors all the clouds around its going down. Pain doesn’t break the calm of the sweet twilight of age, for strength made perfect in weakness bears it all patiently. Ripe fruits of choice experience are gathered as the rare feast of life’s evening, and the soul gets ready for rest.

The Lord’s people will also enjoy light in *the hour of death*. Unbelief mourns: the shadows fall, the night is coming, life is ending. “Ah, no,” cries faith, “the night is far spent, the true day is at hand.” Light has come, the light of immortality, the light of a Father’s face. Gather up your feet into the bed; see the waiting bands of spirits! Angels carry you away. Farewell, dear one, you are gone; you wave your hand. Ah, now it is light. The pearly gates are open; the golden streets shine in the jasper light. We cover our eyes, but you see the unseen. Goodbye, brother; you have light at evening, such as we don’t have yet.

modern:
“If any man sin, we *have* an advocate.” Yes, though we sin, we still have him. John doesn’t say, “If any man sin he has forfeited his advocate,” but “we *have* an advocate,” sinners though we are. All the sin a believer has ever done, or can be allowed to commit, can’t destroy his share in the Lord Jesus Christ as his advocate. The name given to our Lord here is full of meaning. “*Jesus*.” Ah, then he’s just the advocate we need, for Jesus is the name of one whose business and delight it is to save. “They shall call his name Jesus, for *he shall save* his people from their sins.” His sweetest name promises his success.

Next, it is “Jesus *Christ*”: *Christos*, the anointed one. This shows *his authority* to plead. The Christ has a right to plead, for he is the Father’s own appointed advocate and chosen priest. If we had chosen him, he might fail, but if God has laid help on one who is mighty, we may safely lay our trouble where God has laid his help. He is Christ, and so he has authority; he is Christ, and so he is *qualified*, for the anointing has fully fitted him for his work. He can plead in a way that moves the heart of God and wins. What tender words, what persuasive sentences the anointed one will use when he stands up to plead for me!

One more part of his name remains: “Jesus Christ *the righteous*.” This is not only his character but his plea. It is his character, and if the Righteous One is my advocate, then my case is good, or he wouldn’t have taken it up. It is his plea, for he answers the charge of unrighteousness against me by pleading that *he* is righteous. He declares himself my substitute and credits his obedience to my account. My soul, you have a friend perfectly suited to be your advocate. He can’t fail; leave yourself entirely in his hands.

modern:
All the strength our gracious God supplies us with is meant for service, not for self-indulgence or boasting. When the prophet Elijah found the cake baked on the coals and the jar of water placed at his head as he lay under the juniper tree, he wasn’t some gentleman being treated to fine food so he could stretch out and take it easy. Far from it: he was sent to travel forty days and forty nights in the strength of it, on his way to Horeb, the mountain of God. When the Master invited the disciples to “Come and dine” with him, after the meal was over he said to Peter, “Feed my sheep,” and added, “Follow me.” It’s the same with us; we eat the bread of heaven so that we may spend our strength in the Master’s service. We come to the Passover and eat the Passover lamb with our belts fastened and staff in hand, ready to set off as soon as we have satisfied our hunger. Some Christians are all for living on Christ, but aren’t so eager to live *for* Christ. Earth should be a preparation for heaven, and heaven is the place where saints feast most and work most. They sit down at our Lord’s table, and they serve him day and night in his temple. They eat heavenly food and give perfect service.

Believer, work for Christ in the strength you gain from him every day. Some of us still have much to learn about our Lord’s purpose in giving us his grace. We’re not to keep the precious grains of truth the way an Egyptian mummy held wheat for ages, without giving it a chance to grow: we must sow it and water it. Why does the Lord send rain on the thirsty earth and give the warm sunshine? Isn’t it so that these may all help the fruits of the earth to produce food for people? In the same way, the Lord feeds and refreshes our souls so that we may then use our renewed strength to promote his glory.

modern:
Mr. MacDonald asked the people of the island of St. Kilda how a person must be saved. An old man replied, “We shall be saved if we repent, and forsake our sins, and turn to God.” “Yes,” said a middle-aged woman, “and with a true heart too.” “Aye,” added a third, “and with prayer”; and a fourth added, “It must be the prayer of the heart.” “And we must be diligent too,” said a fifth, “in keeping the commandments.” So, each having put in his small coin, and feeling that they had put together a very decent creed, they all looked and listened for the preacher’s approval; but they had stirred his deepest pity. The natural mind always maps out a way for itself in which self can work and become great, but the Lord’s way is just the opposite. Believing and being baptized are not matters of merit to boast in; they are so simple that boasting is ruled out, and free grace takes the prize.

Maybe the reader isn’t saved. What’s the reason? Do you think the way of salvation laid down in this verse is doubtful? How can it be, when God has pledged his own word that it’s certain? Do you think it’s too easy? Why, then, don’t you act on it? Its very ease leaves those who neglect it without excuse. To believe is simply to trust, to depend, to rely on Christ Jesus. To be baptized is to submit to the ordinance our Lord fulfilled at the Jordan, which the converts submitted to at Pentecost, and which the jailer obeyed the very night of his conversion. The outward sign doesn’t save, but it shows us our death, burial and resurrection with Jesus, and, like the Lord’s Supper, it is not to be neglected. Reader, do you believe in Jesus? Then, dear friend, put away your fears: you will be saved. Are you still an unbeliever? Then remember that there is only one door, and if you won’t enter by it, you will perish in your sins.

modern:
Whoever believes in Jesus finds enough in his Lord to satisfy him now and to content him forever. The believer isn’t someone whose days are weary for lack of comfort and whose nights are long for lack of a cheering thought, for he finds in his faith such a spring of joy, such a fountain of comfort, that he is content and happy. Put him in a dungeon, and he’ll find good company; place him in a barren wilderness, and he’ll eat the bread of heaven; drive him away from friendship, and he’ll meet the “friend that sticketh closer than a brother.” Wither all his gourds, and he’ll find shade under the Rock of Ages; undermine the foundation of his earthly hopes, and his heart will still be steady, trusting in the Lord. The heart is as impossible to satisfy as the grave until Jesus enters it, and then it is a cup full to overflowing. There is such fullness in Christ that he alone is the believer’s all. The true saint is so completely satisfied with the all-sufficiency of Jesus that he thirsts no more, except for deeper drinks from the living fountain.

That is the sweet way you will thirst, believer. It won’t be a painful thirst, but one of loving desire; you’ll find it a sweet thing to long for a fuller enjoyment of Jesus’ love. Someone long ago said, “I have been sinking my bucket down into the well full often, but now my thirst after Jesus has become so insatiable, that I long to put the well itself to my lips, and drink right on.” Is this how your heart feels now, believer? Do you feel that all your desires are satisfied in Jesus, and that you want nothing now except to know more of him and to have closer fellowship with him? Then keep coming to the fountain, and take the water of life freely. Jesus will never think you take too much, but will always welcome you, saying, “Drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.”

modern:
A strange choice for Moses, but how much stranger the choice of the one who is a prophet like Moses, and greater than he! Our Lord, who is fair as the lily, has entered into marriage with one who confesses she is black, because the sun has looked on her. Angels marvel that the love of Jesus should be set on poor, lost, guilty people. When each believer is filled with a sense of Jesus’ love, he must also be overwhelmed with astonishment that such love should be poured out on someone so completely unworthy of it. Knowing as we do our secret guilt, unfaithfulness and black-heartedness, we melt in grateful wonder at the matchless freeness and sovereignty of grace. Jesus must have found the cause of his love in his own heart; he couldn’t have found it in us, for it isn’t there. Even since our conversion we have been black, though grace has made us lovely. Holy Rutherford said of himself what each of us must sign our names to: “His relation to me is, that I am sick, and he is the Physician of whom I stand in need. Alas! how often I play fast and loose with Christ! He bindeth, I loose; he buildeth, I cast down; I quarrel with Christ, and he agreeth with me twenty times a day!” Most tender and faithful Husband of our souls, go on with your gracious work of making us like you, until you present even us poor Ethiopians to yourself, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing.

Moses met opposition because of his marriage, and both he and his wife were looked on with an evil eye. Can we be surprised if this empty world opposes Jesus and his bride, especially when great sinners are converted? For this is always the Pharisees’ ground for objecting: “This man receiveth sinners.” The old cause of quarrel is still being revived: “Because he had married an Ethiopian woman.”

modern:
Our heavenly Father sends us frequent troubles *to test our faith*. If our faith is worth anything, it will stand the test. Gilt is afraid of fire, but gold isn’t; the *fake* gem dreads being touched by the diamond, but the real jewel fears no test. It’s a poor faith that can trust God only when friends are true, the body is healthy and business is profitable; but that faith is true which holds on to the Lord’s faithfulness when friends are gone, the body is sick, our spirits are low, and the light of our Father’s face is hidden. A faith that can say in the worst trouble, “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him,” is faith born in heaven.

The Lord afflicts his servants *to glorify himself*, for he is greatly glorified in the graces of his people, which are his own handiwork. When “tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope,” the Lord is honored by these growing virtues. We’d never know the music of the harp if the strings were left untouched; nor enjoy the juice of the grape if it weren’t trodden in the winepress; nor discover the sweet scent of cinnamon if it weren’t pressed and beaten; nor feel the warmth of the fire if the coals weren’t completely burned up. The great Workman’s wisdom and power are shown by the trials his vessels of mercy are allowed to pass through.

Present troubles *also help to heighten future joy*. There must be shadows in the picture to bring out the beauty of the lights. Could we be so supremely blessed in heaven if we hadn’t known the curse of sin and the sorrow of earth? Won’t peace be sweeter after conflict, and rest more welcome after work? Won’t the memory of past sufferings add to the bliss of the glorified? There are many other comforting answers to the question we started our short meditation with; let’s think about it all day long.

modern: Reader, this is an important question. Listen to the Christian’s answer, and see if it is yours. “On whom dost thou trust?” “I trust,” says the Christian, “in a triune God. I trust *the Father*, believing that he chose me before the foundation of the world. I trust him to provide for me in his providence, to teach me, to guide me, to correct me if need be, and to bring me home to his own house, where the many mansions are. I trust *the Son*. He is very God of very God, the man Christ Jesus. I trust him to take away all my sins by his own sacrifice, and to clothe me with his perfect righteousness. I trust him to be my Intercessor, to present my prayers and desires before his Father’s throne, and I trust him to be my Advocate at the last great day, to plead my case and to justify me. I trust him for what he is, for what he has done, and for what he has promised yet to do. And I trust *the Holy Spirit*. He has begun to save me from my inborn sins; I trust him to drive them all out. I trust him to curb my temper, to subdue my will, to enlighten my understanding, to check my passions, to comfort my despondency, to help my weakness, to light up my darkness. I trust him to live in me as my life, to reign in me as my King, to make me holy through and through, spirit, soul and body, and then to take me up to live with the saints in light forever.”

Oh, blessed trust! To trust him whose power will never be used up, whose love will never fade, whose kindness will never change, whose faithfulness will never fail, whose wisdom will never be at a loss, and whose perfect goodness can never grow less! Happy are you, reader, if this trust is yours! Trusting like this, you will enjoy sweet peace now and glory hereafter, and the foundation of your trust will never be removed.

modern:
We learn from this story *the need for human means*. The catch of fish was a miracle, yet neither the fisherman nor his boat nor his fishing gear was set aside; all were used to catch the fish. So in saving souls, God works through means; and as long as the present order of grace stands, God will be pleased to save those who believe by the foolishness of preaching. When God works without instruments, no doubt he is glorified; but he himself has chosen the plan of working through instruments, as the way he is most magnified on earth.

*Means on their own are completely useless.* “Master, we have toiled all the night and have taken nothing.” Why was this? Weren’t they fishermen, working at their own trade? Indeed, they were no beginners; they understood the work. Had they gone about it clumsily? No. Had they lacked effort? No, they had toiled. Had they lacked perseverance? No, they had *toiled all the night*. Was there a shortage of fish in the sea? Certainly not, for as soon as the Master came, the fish swam into the net in shoals. What, then, was the reason? Isn’t it because the means themselves have no power apart from the presence of Jesus? “Without him we can do nothing.” But with Christ we can do all things.

*Christ’s presence gives success.* Jesus sat in Peter’s boat, and by a mysterious influence his will drew the fish to the net. When Jesus is lifted up in his church, his presence is the church’s power: the shout of a king is in the middle of her. “I, if I be lifted up, will draw all men unto me.” Let’s go out this morning to our work of fishing for souls, looking up in faith and around us with solemn concern. Let’s work until night comes, and we won’t labor in vain, for he who tells us to let down the net will fill it with fish.

modern: Notice the great mark of true prayer: “*In the Holy Ghost*.” The seed of acceptable worship must come from heaven’s storehouse. Only the prayer that comes from God can go to God. We must shoot the Lord’s arrows back to him. The desire he writes on our heart will move his heart and bring down a blessing, but the desires of the flesh have no power with him.

Praying in the Holy Spirit is praying with *fervency*. Cold prayers ask the Lord not to hear them. Those who don’t plead earnestly don’t plead at all. You might as well talk of lukewarm fire as of lukewarm prayer; it must be red hot. It is praying *perseveringly*. The true petitioner gathers strength as he goes on, and grows more earnest when God delays his answer. The longer the gate stays shut, the harder he uses the knocker, and the longer the angel lingers, the more determined he is never to let him go without the blessing. Tearful, agonizing, unconquerable persistence is beautiful in God’s sight. It means praying *humbly*, for the Holy Spirit never puffs us up with pride. It is his work to convict of sin, and so to bow us down in sorrow and brokenness of spirit. We’ll never sing *Gloria in excelsis* unless we pray to God *De profundis*: we must cry out of the depths, or we’ll never see glory in the highest. It is *loving* prayer. Prayer should be perfumed with love, soaked in love: love for our fellow saints and love for Christ. What’s more, it must be a prayer full of *faith*. A person prevails only as he believes. The Holy Spirit is the author of faith and strengthens it, so that we pray believing God’s promise. Oh, that this blessed combination of excellent graces, priceless and sweet as the merchant’s spices, might be fragrant within us because the Holy Spirit is in our hearts! Most blessed Comforter, use your mighty power within us, helping our weaknesses in prayer.

modern:
In one sense the road to heaven is very safe, but in other ways *there is no road so dangerous*. It is surrounded by difficulties. One false step (and how easy it is to take one, if grace is absent), and down we go. What a slippery path some of us have to walk! How many times we have to cry out with the psalmist, “My feet were almost gone, my steps had well nigh slipped.” If we were strong, sure-footed mountaineers, this wouldn’t matter so much; but in ourselves, *how weak we are*! On the best roads *we soon falter*; on the smoothest paths we quickly stumble. These feeble knees of ours can hardly hold up our tottering weight. A straw may trip us, and a pebble can wound us. We are mere children, trembling as we take our first steps in the walk of faith; our heavenly Father holds us by the arms, or we’d soon be down. Oh, if we are kept from falling, how we must bless the patient power that watches over us day by day! Think how prone we are to sin, how quick to choose danger, how strong our tendency to throw ourselves down, and these thoughts will make us sing more sweetly than we ever have, “Glory be to him, who is able to keep us from falling.”

*We have many enemies* who try to push us down. The road is rough and we are weak, but on top of this, enemies lie in ambush, rushing out when we least expect them and working to trip us up or hurl us over the nearest cliff. Only an almighty arm can protect us from these unseen enemies who are out to destroy us. Such an arm is pledged to defend us. He who promised is faithful, and he is able to keep us from falling. So, with a deep sense of our complete weakness, we may hold on to a firm belief in our perfect safety, and say with joyful confidence:

modern:
Sincere seekers who haven’t yet received the blessing may take comfort from this story. The Savior didn’t give the blessing at once, even though the woman had great faith in him. He meant to give it, but he waited a while. “He answered her not a word.” Weren’t her prayers good? There were never better in the world. Wasn’t her case needy? Sorrowfully needy. Didn’t she *feel* her need enough? She felt it overwhelmingly. Wasn’t she earnest enough? She was intensely earnest. Did she have no faith? She had so much that even Jesus marveled, and said, “O woman, great is thy faith.” See, then: although it’s true that faith brings peace, it doesn’t always bring it instantly. There may be reasons that call for the testing of faith rather than its reward. Real faith may be in the soul like a hidden seed that hasn’t yet budded and blossomed into joy and peace. A painful silence from the Savior is the heavy trial of many a seeking soul, but heavier still is the blow of a harsh, cutting reply like this: “It is not meet to take the children’s bread, and to cast it to dogs.”

Many who wait on the Lord find delight immediately, but that isn’t the case with everyone. Some, like the jailer, are turned from darkness to light in a moment, but others are plants of slower growth. You may be given a deeper sense of sin instead of a sense of pardon, and if so, you’ll need patience to bear the heavy blow. Ah, poor heart, even if Christ beats and bruises you, or even kills you, trust him; even if he gives you an angry word, believe in the love of his heart. Please don’t give up seeking or trusting my Master because you haven’t yet felt the joy you long for. Throw yourself on him, and keep depending on him, even where you can’t yet hope with rejoicing.

modern:
Turn over in your mind that wonderful word: “*faultless*!” We are far from it now; but since our Lord never stops short of perfection in his work of love, we’ll reach it one day. The Savior who will keep his people to the end will also present them at last to himself as “a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing, but holy and without blemish.” All the jewels in the Savior’s crown are of the finest quality and without a single flaw. All the bridesmaids who attend the Lamb’s wife are pure virgins, without spot or stain.

But how will Jesus make us faultless? He will wash us from our sins in his own blood until we are as white and fair as God’s purest angel; and we’ll be clothed in his righteousness, the righteousness that makes the saint who wears it truly faultless; yes, perfect in God’s sight. We’ll be blameless and beyond reproach, even in his eyes. His law will not only have no charge against us, but will be honored in us. What’s more, the work of the Holy Spirit in us will be entirely complete. He will make us so perfectly holy that we’ll have no lingering tendency to sin. Judgment, memory, will: every power and passion will be set free from the slavery of evil. We’ll be holy, just as God is holy, and we’ll live in his presence forever. Saints won’t be out of place in heaven; their beauty will be as great as that of the place prepared for them.

Oh, the rapture of that hour when the everlasting doors are lifted up, and we, made fit for the inheritance, live with the saints in light! Sin gone, Satan shut out, temptation past forever, and ourselves “faultless” before God: this will be heaven indeed! Let’s be joyful now as we rehearse the song of eternal praise that will so soon roll out in full chorus from the whole blood-washed host. Let’s copy David’s dancing for joy before the ark as a prelude to our ecstasies before the throne.

modern:
Notice how gloriously personal the promise is. *I* will, *I* will. The Lord Jehovah himself steps in to rescue and redeem his people. He pledges himself personally to rescue them. His own arm will do it, so that he may have the glory. Not a word is said here about any effort of ours that might be needed to help the Lord. Neither our strength nor our weakness is taken into account, but the lone *I*, like the sun in the sky, shines out in splendor, sufficient for everything. Why, then, do we count up our forces and consult with flesh and blood, to our own painful hurt? Jehovah has power enough without borrowing from our puny arm. Peace, you unbelieving thoughts! Be still, and know that the Lord reigns.

Nor is there a hint about secondary means and causes. The Lord says nothing about friends and helpers: he takes on the work alone and feels no need of human arms to help him. All our looking around to companions and relatives is useless; they are broken reeds if we lean on them, often unwilling when they’re able, and unable when they’re willing. Since the promise comes from God alone, we’d do well to wait only on him; and when we do, our hope never lets us down.

Who are the wicked, that we should fear them? The Lord will wipe them out completely; they’re to be pitied rather than feared. As for the terrible ones, they are only terrors to those who have no God to run to, for when the Lord is on our side, whom shall we fear? If we rush into sin to please the wicked, we have reason to be alarmed; but if we hold on to our integrity, the rage of tyrants will be overruled for our good. When the fish swallowed Jonah, it found him a mouthful it couldn’t digest; and when the world devours the church, it’s glad to be rid of it again. In every time of fiery trial, let’s keep possession of our souls with patience.

modern:
Prayer *teaches us our unworthiness*, a very healthy lesson for proud creatures like us. If God gave us favors without making us pray for them, we’d never know how poor we are; but a true prayer is an inventory of wants, a catalog of needs, an uncovering of hidden poverty. While it applies to God’s wealth, it confesses human emptiness. The healthiest state for a Christian is to be always empty in himself and constantly depending on the Lord for supplies; always poor in himself and rich in Jesus; weak as water personally, but mighty through God to do great deeds. And that is the use of prayer: while it adores God, it puts the creature where it belongs, in the very dust.

Prayer in itself, apart from the answer it brings, is a great benefit to the Christian. As a runner gains strength for the race by daily exercise, so for the great race of life we gain energy by the holy work of prayer. Prayer grows the feathers on the wings of God’s young eagles, so that they learn to soar above the clouds. Prayer straps on the armor of God’s warriors and sends them out to battle with their sinews braced and their muscles firm. An earnest pleader comes out of his prayer room as the sun rises from the chambers of the east, rejoicing like a strong man to run his race. Prayer is that raised hand of Moses which defeats the Amalekites more than Joshua’s sword; it is the arrow shot from the prophet’s window, foretelling defeat for the Syrians. Prayer clothes human weakness with divine strength, turns human folly into heavenly wisdom, and gives troubled mortals the peace of God. We don’t know what prayer can’t do! We thank you, great God, for the mercy-seat, a choice proof of your marvelous loving-kindness. Help us to use it rightly all through this day!

modern:
In the second letter to Timothy, chapter one, verse nine, are these words: “Who hath saved us, and called us with an *holy* calling.” Now here is a touchstone for testing our calling. It is “an holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace.” This calling forbids all trust in our own doings and leads us to Christ alone for salvation, but afterward it cleanses us from dead works to serve the living and true God. As he who called you is holy, so you must be holy. If you are living in sin, you aren’t called; but if you truly belong to Christ, you can say, “Nothing pains me as much as sin. I want to be rid of it. Lord, help me to be holy.” Is this what your heart longs for? Is this the course of your life toward God and his will?

Again, in [[Phil.3.13-Phil.3.14|Philippians 3:13–14]], we read of “The *high* calling of God in Christ Jesus.” Is your calling, then, a high calling? Has it ennobled your heart and set it on heavenly things? Has it raised your hopes, your tastes, your desires? Has it lifted the steady course of your life, so that you spend it with God and for God?

We find another test in [[Heb.3.1|Hebrews 3:1]]: “Partakers of the *heavenly* calling.” A heavenly calling means a call *from* heaven. If man alone calls you, you aren’t called. Is your calling from God? Is it a call *to* heaven as well as from heaven? Unless you are a stranger here and heaven is your home, you haven’t been called with a heavenly calling; for those who have been called that way declare that they look for a city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God, and that they themselves are strangers and pilgrims on the earth. Is your calling holy, high and heavenly like this? Then, dear friend, you have been called by God, for this is the calling with which God calls his people.

modern:
There are times when solitude is better than company, and silence wiser than speech. We would be better Christians if we were alone more, waiting on God and gathering spiritual strength, through meditation on his Word, for work in his service. We ought to *think deeply about the things of God, because that’s how we get the real nourishment out of them*. Truth is something like a cluster of grapes: if we want wine from it, we must crush it; we must press and squeeze it many times. The treader’s feet must come down joyfully on the bunches, or the juice won’t flow; and they must tread the grapes well, or much of the precious liquid will be wasted. So we must tread the clusters of truth by meditation, if we want to get the wine of comfort from them.

Our bodies aren’t kept alive merely by putting food in our mouths; the process that really supplies the muscle, the nerve, the sinew and the bone is digestion. It is by digestion that the food outside us becomes part of the life inside us. Our souls aren’t nourished merely by listening for a while to this part of God’s truth, then to that, and then to another. Hearing, reading, marking and learning all need inward digesting to complete their usefulness, and the inward digesting of the truth lies mostly in meditating on it. Why is it that some Christians, though they hear many sermons, make only slow progress in the Christian life? Because they neglect their prayer rooms and don’t thoughtfully meditate on God’s Word. They love the wheat, but they don’t grind it; they would have the grain, but won’t go out into the fields to gather it; the fruit hangs on the tree, but they won’t pick it; the water flows at their feet, but they won’t stoop to drink it. Lord, deliver us from such folly, and let this be our resolution this morning: *“I will meditate in thy precepts.”*

modern:
This age is especially the age of the Holy Spirit, in which Jesus cheers us not by his bodily presence, as he will by and by, but by the Holy Spirit living in us and constantly staying with us, who is always the Comforter of the church. It is his work to console the hearts of God’s people. He convicts of sin; he enlightens and instructs; but still the main part of his work lies in gladdening the hearts of the renewed, strengthening the weak and lifting up all who are bowed down. He does this by revealing Jesus to them. The Holy Spirit consoles, but Christ *is the consolation*. If we may use the picture, the Holy Spirit is the Physician, but Jesus is the medicine. *He* heals the wound, but he does it by applying the holy ointment of Christ’s name and grace. He doesn’t take from his own things, but from the things of Christ. So if we give the Holy Spirit the Greek name *Paraclete*, as we sometimes do, then our heart gives our blessed Lord Jesus the title *Paraclesis*. If the one is the Comforter, the other is the Comfort.

Now, with such rich provision for his need, why should a Christian be sad and discouraged? The Holy Spirit has graciously pledged to be your Comforter. Do you imagine, weak and trembling believer, that he will neglect his sacred trust? Can you suppose he has taken on something he can’t or won’t carry out? If it’s his special work to strengthen and comfort you, do you suppose he has forgotten his business, or that he’ll fail in the loving work he has taken up for you? No, don’t think so harshly of the tender and blessed Spirit whose name is “the Comforter.” He delights to give the oil of joy for mourning and the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. Trust him, and he will surely comfort you until the house of mourning is closed forever and the marriage feast has begun.

modern: Genuine, spiritual mourning over sin is *the work of the Spirit of God*. Repentance is too choice a flower to grow in nature’s garden. Pearls grow naturally in oysters, but penitence never shows up in sinners unless God’s grace produces it in them. If you have one particle of real hatred for sin, God must have given it to you, for the thorns of human nature never produced a single fig. “That which is born of the flesh is flesh.”

True repentance *looks clearly to the Savior*. When we repent of sin, we must have one eye on the sin and the other on the cross; or better still, we should fix both eyes on Christ and see our sins only in the light of his love.

True sorrow for sin is *intensely practical*. No one can say he hates sin if he lives in it. Repentance makes us see the evil of sin, not merely in theory but by experience, the way a burned child dreads fire. We’ll be as afraid of it as a man who has just been held up and robbed is afraid of the thief on the highway; and we’ll avoid it, avoid it in everything, not only in great things but in little things, as people avoid little vipers as well as big snakes. True mourning for sin will make us very watchful over our tongue, in case it says a wrong word. We’ll keep a close eye on our daily actions, in case we offend in anything; each night we’ll close the day with painful confessions of falling short, and each morning wake up with anxious prayers that God would hold us up today, so that we don’t sin against him.

Sincere repentance is *continual*. Believers repent until their dying day. This dripping well never stops. Every other sorrow gives way to time, but this dear sorrow grows as we grow, and it is such a sweet bitterness that we thank God we are allowed to enjoy and suffer it until we enter our eternal rest.

modern: Whose love can this be, which is as mighty as death, the conqueror of kings and destroyer of the human race? Wouldn’t it sound like mockery if it were said of my poor, weak and barely living love for Jesus my Lord? I do love him, and perhaps by his grace I could even die for him; but as for my love in itself, it can hardly stand a scoffing joke, let alone a cruel death. Surely it is my Beloved’s love that is spoken of here: the love of Jesus, the matchless lover of souls. His love was indeed stronger than the most terrible death, for it went through the trial of the cross in triumph. It was a lingering death, but love outlasted the torment; a shameful death, but love despised the shame; a death as punishment, but love carried our sins; a forsaken, lonely death, from which the eternal Father hid his face, but love endured the curse and triumphed over everything. There was never such love, never such a death. It was a desperate duel, but love won the prize. What then, my heart? Is nothing stirred in you as you think about such heavenly love? Yes, my Lord, I long, I pant, to feel your love blazing like a furnace inside me. Come yourself and kindle my spirit’s fire.

Why should I despair of loving Jesus with a love as strong as death? He deserves it; I want it. The martyrs felt such love, and they were only flesh and blood, so why not I? They mourned their weakness, and yet out of weakness were made strong. Grace gave them all their unflinching steadfastness, and there is the same grace for me. Jesus, lover of my soul, pour out such love, your own love, in my heart this evening.

modern:
Spiritual knowledge of Christ will be *personal* knowledge. I can’t know Jesus through someone else’s acquaintance with him. No, I must know him *myself*; I must know him for myself. It will be *intelligent* knowledge: I must know *him*, not as the dreamer imagines him, but as the Word reveals him. I must know his natures, divine and human. I must know his offices, his attributes, his works, his shame, his glory. I must meditate on him until I “comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; and know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge.” It will be *affectionate* knowledge of him; in fact, if I know him at all, I must love him. An ounce of heart knowledge is worth a ton of head learning.

Our knowledge of him will be *satisfying* knowledge. When I know my Savior, my mind will be full to the brim; I’ll feel I have what my spirit longed for. “This is that bread whereof if a man eat he shall never hunger.” At the same time it will be *stirring* knowledge: the more I know of my Beloved, the more I’ll want to know. The higher I climb, the loftier the peaks that invite my eager steps. The more I get, the more I’ll want. Like the miser’s treasure, my gold will make me covet more.

To finish: this knowledge of Christ Jesus will be a most *happy* one. In fact, it lifts me so high that sometimes it will carry me completely above all trials and doubts and sorrows. And while I enjoy it, it will make me something more than “Man that is born of woman, who is of few days, and full of trouble”; for it will wrap me in the immortality of the ever-living Savior, and tie around me the golden belt of his eternal joy. Come, my soul, sit at Jesus’ feet and learn from him all day today.

modern:
If a Christian can possibly be saved while he conforms to this world, at any rate it must be “so as by fire.” Such a bare escape is almost as much to be dreaded as desired. Reader, would you like to leave this world in the darkness of a despairing deathbed, and enter heaven the way a shipwrecked sailor climbs the rocks of his home country? Then be worldly; mix with the worshipers of money, and refuse to go outside the camp bearing Christ’s reproach. But would you have a heaven below as well as a heaven above? Would you grasp with all the saints what are the heights and depths, and know the love of Christ which passes knowledge? Would you receive an abundant entrance into the joy of your Lord? Then come out from among them, and be separate, and don’t touch the unclean thing.

Would you reach the full assurance of faith? You can’t gain it while you keep close company with sinners. Would you blaze with fervent love? Your love will be dampened by the drenchings of godless company. You can’t become a great Christian. You may be a baby in grace, but you can never be a mature man in Christ Jesus while you give yourself up to the worldly maxims and business ways of the people of this world. It’s bad for an heir of heaven to be close friends with the heirs of hell. It looks bad when a courtier is too friendly with his king’s enemies. Even small inconsistencies are dangerous. Little thorns make great blisters, little moths destroy fine clothes, and little frivolities and little dishonesties will rob religion of a thousand joys. Oh, professing Christian, too little separated from sinners, you don’t know what you lose by conforming to the world. It cuts the tendons of your strength and makes you crawl where you ought to run. So, for your own comfort’s sake, and for the sake of your growth in grace, if you are a Christian, be a Christian, and be a marked and distinct one.

modern:
His first coming was without outward pomp or show of power, and yet in fact few could stand its testing power. Herod and all Jerusalem with him were stirred up at the news of the wonderful birth. Those who thought they were waiting for him showed how false their claims were by rejecting him when he came. His life on earth was a winnowing fan that tested the great heap of religious profession, and few enough could survive the process. But what will his second coming be like? What sinner can bear to think of it? “He shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked.” When, in his humiliation, he only said to the soldiers, “I am he,” they fell backward. What will the terror of his enemies be when he reveals himself more fully as the “*I am*”? His death shook the earth and darkened the sky; what will be the dreadful splendor of the day when, as the living Savior, he summons the living and the dead before him?

Oh, that the terrors of the Lord would persuade people to give up their sins and kiss the Son, in case he is angry! Though a lamb, he is still the lion of the tribe of Judah, tearing the prey to pieces; and though he doesn’t break the bruised reed, he will break his enemies with a rod of iron and smash them like a potter’s jar. None of his enemies will stand up before the storm of his wrath, or hide from the sweeping hail of his anger; but his dearly loved people, washed in his blood, look for his appearing with joy and hope to stand it without fear. To them he sits as a refiner even now, and when he has tested them, they will come out as gold. Let’s search ourselves this morning and make our calling and election sure, so that the coming of the Lord stirs no dark forebodings in our minds. Oh, for grace to throw away all hypocrisy, and to be found by him sincere and without blame on the day of his appearing!

modern:
Every firstborn creature had to be the Lord’s, but since the donkey was unclean, it couldn’t be offered in sacrifice. What then? Should it be let off from the universal law? Certainly not. God allows no exceptions. The donkey is his due, but he won’t accept it; he won’t lower his claim, and yet he can’t be pleased with that victim. There was no way of escape left but redemption: the creature had to be saved by putting a lamb in its place; or if it wasn’t redeemed, it had to die. My soul, here is a lesson for you. That unclean animal is you. You rightly belong to the Lord who made you and keeps you, but you are so sinful that God will not, cannot, accept you; and it has come to this: the Lamb of God must stand in your place, or you must die forever. Let all the world know how grateful you are to that spotless Lamb who has already bled for you, and so redeemed you from the deadly curse of the law.

Mustn’t the Israelite sometimes have wondered which should die, the donkey or the lamb? Wouldn’t a good man stop to weigh and compare? Surely there was no comparison between the value of a human soul and the life of the Lord Jesus, and yet the Lamb dies, and man, the donkey, is spared. My soul, marvel at God’s boundless love for you and for others of the human race. Worms are bought with the blood of the Son of the Highest! Dust and ashes redeemed with a price far above silver and gold! What a doom would have been mine if plenteous redemption hadn’t been found! Breaking the donkey’s neck was only a momentary penalty, but who can measure the wrath to come, which has no imaginable limit? Precious beyond all reckoning is the glorious Lamb who has redeemed us from such a doom.

modern:
In these words the believer is invited to a holy closeness to Jesus. “Come and dine” suggests the same table and the same food; yes, and sometimes it means sitting side by side and leaning our head on the Savior’s chest. It is being brought into the banqueting house, where the banner of redeeming love waves. “Come and dine” gives us a picture of *union with Jesus*, because the only food we can feast on when we dine with Jesus is *himself*. Oh, what union this is! That we feed on Jesus like this is a depth reason can’t measure. “He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him.”

It is also an invitation to enjoy *fellowship with the saints*. Christians may differ on a variety of points, but they all have one spiritual appetite; and if we can’t all *feel* alike, we can all *feed* alike on the bread of life sent down from heaven. At the table of fellowship with Jesus we are one bread and one cup. As the loving cup goes round, we heartily drink to one another from it. Get closer to Jesus, and you’ll find yourself linked more and more in spirit to all who are like you, kept alive by the same heavenly manna. If we were closer to Jesus, we’d be closer to one another.

We also see in these words the *source of strength* for every Christian. To look at Christ is to live, but for strength to serve him you must “come and dine.” We work under a great deal of unnecessary weakness because we neglect this command of the Master. None of us needs to put himself on a starvation diet; on the contrary, we should grow fat on the rich food of the gospel, so that we may build up strength from it and stretch every power to the full in the Master’s service. So, then, if you want to know *closeness* to Jesus, *union* with Jesus, *love* for his people and *strength from Jesus*, “come and dine” with him by faith.

modern:
There are times in our spiritual experience when human advice or sympathy, or the ordinances of religion, fail to comfort or help us. Why does our gracious God allow this? Perhaps because we have been living too much without him, and so he takes away everything we have been in the habit of depending on, to drive us to himself. It is a blessed thing to live at the fountainhead. While our water skins are full, we are content, like Hagar and Ishmael, to go into the wilderness; but when they’re dry, nothing will do for us but “Thou God seest me.” We are like the prodigal: we love the pig troughs and forget our Father’s house. Remember, we can make pig troughs and husks even out of the forms of religion. They are blessed things, but we may put them in God’s place, and then they’re worthless. Anything becomes an idol when it keeps us away from God: even the bronze serpent is to be despised as “Nehushtan” if we worship it instead of God. The prodigal was never safer than when he was driven into his father’s arms, because he could find food nowhere else. Our Lord does us the favor of a famine in the land, to make us seek him all the more.

The best position for a Christian is living wholly and directly on God’s grace, still standing where he stood at first: “Having nothing, and yet possessing all things.” Let’s never for a moment think that our standing depends on our sanctification, our putting sin to death, our graces or our feelings. Let’s know instead that we are saved because Christ offered a full atonement, for we are complete in him. We have nothing of our own to trust in, but rest on the merits of Jesus: his suffering and his holy life give us the only sure ground of confidence. Dear friend, when we are brought to a state of thirst, we’re sure to turn eagerly to the fountain of life.

modern:
The thought in David’s heart at this time was a *false* thought, because he certainly had no reason to think that God’s anointing him through Samuel was meant to be left an empty, meaningless act. Not once had the Lord deserted his servant. He had very often been put in dangerous positions, but there wasn’t one case in which God hadn’t stepped in and rescued him. The trials he had faced had been varied; they hadn’t taken one form only, but many; yet in every case the one who sent the trial had also graciously provided a way of escape. David couldn’t put his finger on any entry in his diary and say of it, “Here is evidence that the Lord will forsake me,” for the whole course of his past life proved the very opposite. He should have reasoned from what God *had* done for him that God would still be his defender.

But isn’t it just the same way that *we* doubt God’s help? Isn’t it *mistrust without a cause*? Have we ever had the shadow of a reason to doubt our Father’s goodness? Hasn’t his loving-kindness been marvelous? Has he *once* failed to justify our trust? Ah, no! Our God hasn’t left us at any time. We have had dark nights, but the star of love has shone out in the blackness; we have been in hard battles, but he has held the shield of our defense high over our head. We have gone through many trials, but never to our harm, always to our good; and the conclusion from our past experience is that he who has been with us in six troubles won’t forsake us in the seventh. What we have known of our faithful God proves that he will keep us to the end. So let’s not reason against the evidence. How can we ever be so ungenerous as to *doubt* our God? Lord, throw down the Jezebel of our unbelief, and let the dogs devour it.

modern:
Our good Shepherd has sheep of many kinds of experience in his flock: some are strong in the Lord, and others are weak in faith; but he is impartial in caring for all his sheep, and the weakest lamb is as dear to him as the most mature of the flock. Lambs tend to lag behind, are prone to wander and quick to grow tired, but the Shepherd protects them from all the dangers of these weaknesses with his powerful arm. He finds newborn souls, like young lambs, ready to die, and he feeds them until their life grows strong; he finds weak minds ready to faint and die, and he comforts them and renews their strength. He gathers all the little ones, for it isn’t the will of our heavenly Father that one of them should perish. What a quick eye he must have to see them all! What a tender heart to care for them all! What a far-reaching and powerful arm to gather them all! In his lifetime on earth he was a great gatherer of the weaker sort, and now that he lives in heaven, his loving heart still yearns over the meek and contrite, the timid and feeble, the fearful and fainting here below.

How gently he gathered me to himself, to his truth, to his blood, to his love, to his church! With what effective grace he compelled me to come to him! Since I was first converted, how often he has brought me back from my wanderings and folded me again within the circle of his everlasting arm! Best of all, he does it all himself, personally. He doesn’t hand the task of love to someone else, but stoops himself to rescue and keep his most unworthy servant. How can I love him enough, or serve him as he deserves? I would gladly make his name great to the ends of the earth, but what can my weakness do for him? Great Shepherd, add this one more mercy to all the others: a heart to love you more truly, as I ought.

modern: Many are “the paths of the Lord” that “drop fatness,” but one in particular is the *path of prayer*. No believer who spends much time in his prayer room will need to cry, “My leanness, my leanness; woe unto me.” Starving souls live far from the mercy-seat, and become like parched fields in a drought. Prevailing with God in wrestling prayer is sure to make the believer strong, if not happy. The nearest place to the gate of heaven is the throne of heavenly grace. Spend much time alone with Jesus, and you’ll have much assurance; spend little time alone with him, and your religion will be shallow, polluted with many doubts and fears, and not sparkling with the joy of the Lord. Since the soul-enriching path of prayer is open to the very weakest saint; since no high attainments are required; since you aren’t told to come because you’re an advanced saint, but are freely invited if you are a saint at all; make sure, dear reader, that you often take the road of private prayer. Spend much time on your knees, for that is how Elijah brought the rain down on starving Israel’s fields.

There is another special path dripping with richness for those who walk in it: the secret walk of fellowship. Oh, the delights of fellowship with Jesus! Earth has no words to describe the holy calm of a soul leaning on Jesus’ chest. Few Christians understand it. They live in the lowlands and seldom climb to the top of Nebo; they live in the outer court and don’t enter the holy place; they don’t take up the privilege of priesthood. They see the sacrifice from a distance, but they don’t sit down with the priest to eat it and enjoy the fat of the burnt offering. But you, reader, sit always under the shadow of Jesus. Come up to that palm tree and take hold of its branches; let your beloved be to you like the apple tree among the trees of the wood, and you’ll be satisfied as with marrow and fatness. O Jesus, visit us with your salvation!

modern:
Saul had been commanded to destroy all the Amalekites and their cattle completely. Instead, he spared the king and let his people take the best of the oxen and sheep. When he was called to account for it, he declared that he had done it to offer sacrifices to God; but Samuel answered him at once that sacrifices were no excuse for an act of open rebellion. The sentence before us deserves to be printed in letters of gold and hung up before the eyes of the present idol-worshiping generation, who are very fond of the finery of self-invented worship but utterly neglect the laws of God. Always remember that keeping strictly to the path of your Savior’s command is better than any outward form of religion, and listening to his teaching with an attentive ear is better than bringing the fat of rams, or any other precious thing, to lay on his altar.

If you are failing to keep the least of Christ’s commands to his disciples, I beg you, don’t be disobedient any longer. All your claims of devotion to your Master, and all the religious acts you may perform, are no compensation for disobedience. “To obey,” even in the slightest and smallest thing, “is better than sacrifice,” however grand. Don’t talk about Gregorian chants, rich robes, incense and banners. The first thing God requires of his child is obedience; and though you were to give your body to be burned, and all your goods to feed the poor, if you don’t listen to the Lord’s commands, all your ceremonies will do you no good. It’s a blessed thing to be teachable as a little child, but it’s much more blessed, once the lesson is taught, to carry it out to the letter. How many decorate their temples and dress up their priests, but refuse to obey the word of the Lord! My soul, have no part in their counsel.

modern:
Are you mourning, believer, because you are so weak in the Christian life, because your faith is so small and your love so feeble? Cheer up, for you have reason to be grateful. Remember *that in some things you are equal to the greatest and most mature Christian*. You are as much bought with blood as he is. You are as much an adopted child of God as any other believer. A baby is as truly its parents’ child as a grown man. You are as completely justified, for justification doesn’t come in degrees: your little faith has made you clean every bit. You have as much right to the precious things of the covenant as the most advanced believers, for your right to covenant mercies lies not in your growth, but in the covenant itself; and your faith in Jesus isn’t the measure but the proof of your inheritance in him. You are as rich as the richest, if not in enjoyment, then in actual possession. The smallest star that gleams is set in heaven; the faintest ray of light is related to the great sun. In glory’s family register, the small and the great are written with the same pen.

You are as dear to your Father’s heart as the greatest in the family. Jesus is very tender toward you. You are like the smoldering wick; a rougher spirit would say, “Put out that smoking flax; it fills the room with an offensive smell!” but the smoldering wick *he* will not put out. You are like a bruised reed; any hand less tender than the Chief Musician’s would step on you or throw you away, but he will never break the bruised reed. Instead of being downcast because of what you are, you should triumph in Christ. Am I only small in Israel? Yet in Christ I am made to sit in heavenly places. Am I poor in faith? Still, in Jesus I am heir of all things. Though “less than nothing I can boast, and vanity confess,” yet if the root of the matter is in me, I will rejoice in the Lord and glory in the God of my salvation.

modern:
Anyone can sing in the daytime. When the cup is full, a person draws inspiration from it. When wealth pours in around him, anyone can praise the God who gives a plentiful harvest or brings home a loaded ship. It’s easy enough for a wind harp to whisper music when the wind blows; the difficulty is for music to swell out when no wind is stirring. It’s easy to sing when we can read the notes by daylight; but the skilled singer is the one who sings when there isn’t a ray of light to read by, who sings from his heart. No one can make a song in the night by himself. He may try, but he’ll find that a song in the night must be inspired by God. Let everything go well, and I can weave songs, fashioning them wherever I go out of the flowers that grow along my path; but put me in a desert where nothing green grows, and what will I make a hymn of praise to God from? How can a mortal make a crown for the Lord where there are no jewels? Just let this voice be clear and this body full of health, and I can sing God’s praise; but silence my tongue, lay me on a sickbed, and how will I sing God’s high praises then, unless he himself gives me the song?

No, it isn’t in human power to sing when everything is against us, unless a coal from the altar touches our lips. It was a divine song Habakkuk sang when in the night he said, “Although the fig-tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in the Lord, I will joy in the God of my salvation.” Then, since our Maker gives *songs in the night*, let’s wait on him for the music. O Chief Musician, don’t let us stay songless because trouble is on us, but tune our lips to the melody of thanksgiving.

modern:
Many Christians stay stunted and dwarfed in spiritual things, looking just the same year after year. No new growth of deeper and finer feeling shows in them. They exist, but they don’t “*grow up into him in all things*.” But should we rest content with being the “green blade” when we might move on to “the ear,” and finally ripen into the “full corn in the ear”? Should we be satisfied to believe in Christ and say, “I am safe,” without wanting to know more, in our own experience, of the fullness that’s found in him? It shouldn’t be like that. Like good traders in heaven’s market, we should be eager to grow rich in the knowledge of Jesus. It’s all very well to keep other people’s vineyards, but we mustn’t neglect our own spiritual growth and ripening. Why should it always be winter in our hearts? We must have our seedtime, it’s true, but oh, for a springtime, yes, a summer season that promises an early harvest!

If we want to ripen in grace, we must live close to Jesus, in his presence, ripened by the sunshine of his smiles. We must have sweet fellowship with him. We must leave the distant view of his face and come near, as John did, and rest our head on his chest; then we’ll find ourselves growing in holiness, in love, in faith, in hope, yes, in every precious gift. The sun rises first on the mountaintops and gilds them with its light, one of the most charming sights a traveler can see. In the same way, one of the most delightful things in the world to think about is the glow of the Spirit’s light on the head of some saint who has grown in spiritual stature, like Saul, above his fellows, until, like a mighty snow-capped Alp, he is the first among the chosen to reflect the beams of the Sun of Righteousness, and carries the shine of its brightness high up for everyone to see, and, seeing it, to glorify his Father who is in heaven.

modern: Although this message was sent to the south and referred to the descendants of Israel, it can usefully be a summons to us too. We are naturally slow to all good things, and it’s a lesson of grace to learn to go forward in God’s ways. Reader, are you unconverted, but do you want to trust in the Lord Jesus? Then *don’t hold back*. Love invites you, the promises guarantee your success, the precious blood prepares the way. Don’t let sins or fears hold you back, but come to Jesus just as you are. Do you long to pray? Would you pour out your heart before the Lord? *Don’t hold back*. The mercy-seat is ready for those who need mercy; a sinner’s cries will prevail with God. You are invited; no, you are commanded to pray. So come boldly to the throne of grace.

Dear friend, are you already saved? Then *don’t hold back* from joining with the Lord’s people. Don’t neglect the ordinances of baptism and the Lord’s Supper. You may be timid by nature, but you must fight against it, in case it leads you into disobedience. There’s a sweet promise made to those who confess Christ; don’t miss it on any account, in case you come under the condemnation of those who deny him. If you have talents, *don’t hold back* from using them. Don’t hoard your wealth or waste your time; don’t let your abilities rust or your influence go unused. Jesus didn’t hold back; imitate him by being first in self-denial and self-sacrifice. *Don’t hold back* from close fellowship with God, from boldly claiming covenant blessings, from growing in the Christian life, from looking into the precious mysteries of Christ’s love. And, dear friend, don’t be guilty of holding others back by your coldness, harshness or suspicion. For Jesus’ sake, go forward yourself, and encourage others to do the same. Hell and the allied armies of superstition and unbelief are eager for the fight. O soldiers of the cross, don’t hold back!

modern:
How much do you owe my Lord? Has he ever done anything for you? Has he forgiven your sins? Has he covered you with a robe of righteousness? Has he set your feet on a rock? Has he made your steps firm? Has he prepared heaven for you? Has he prepared you for heaven? Has he written your name in his book of life? Has he given you countless blessings? Has he stored up mercies for you which eye has not seen nor ear heard? Then do something for Jesus worthy of his love. Don’t give a dying Redeemer an offering of mere words. How will you feel when your Master comes, if you have to confess that you *did* nothing for him, but kept your love shut up like a stagnant pool, never flowing out to his poor or to his work? Away with love like that! What do people think of a love that never shows itself in action? Why, they say, “Open rebuke is better than secret love.” Who will accept a love so weak that it doesn’t move you to a single act of self-denial, generosity, heroism or zeal? Think how *he* has loved you and given himself for you!

Do you know the power of that love? Then let it be like a rushing mighty wind in your soul, sweeping out the clouds of your worldliness and clearing away the mists of sin. Let “For Christ’s sake” be the tongue of fire that rests on you; let “for Christ’s sake” be the divine rapture, the heavenly breath of inspiration that carries you up from earth, the divine spirit that makes you bold as lions and swift as eagles in your Lord’s service. Love should give wings to the feet of service and strength to the arms of work. Fixed on God with a steadiness that can’t be shaken, determined to honor him with a resolve that won’t be turned aside, and pressing on with a passion that never tires, let’s show how the love of Jesus compels us. May that divine magnet draw us heavenward to itself.

modern:
“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest O Israel, my way is hid from the Lord, and my judgment is passed over from my God?” The Lord cares for everything, and the lowliest creatures share in his universal providence, but his particular providence is over his saints. “The angel of the Lord encampeth round about them that fear him.” “Precious shall their blood be in his sight.” “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” “We know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them that are the called according to his purpose.” Let it cheer and comfort you that, while he is the Savior of all people, he is especially the Savior of those who believe. You are his special care: his royal treasure, which he guards like the apple of his eye; his vineyard, which he watches over day and night. “The very hairs of your head are all numbered.” Let the thought of his special love *for you* be a spiritual painkiller, a dear end to your sorrow: “I will never leave *thee*, nor forsake *thee*.” God says that as much to you as to any saint of old. “Fear not, I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward.”

We lose a lot of comfort by the habit of reading his promises as meant for the whole church, instead of taking them straight home to ourselves. Believer, grasp God’s word with a personal faith that makes it your own. Imagine you hear Jesus say, “I have prayed for *thee* that thy faith fail not.” Imagine you see him walking on the waters of your trouble, for he is there, and he is saying, “Fear not, it is I; be not afraid.” Oh, those sweet words of Christ! May the Holy Spirit make you feel them as spoken to *you*. Forget others for a while; accept the voice of Jesus as addressed to you, and say, “Jesus whispers consolation; I cannot refuse it; I will sit under his shadow with great delight.”

modern:
This sentence is a whole system of theology in miniature. Whoever understands its meaning is a theologian, and whoever can dive into its fullness is a true master in Israel. It is a summary of the glorious message of salvation that was delivered to us in Christ Jesus our Redeemer. The meaning hinges on the word “freely.” This is the glorious, the fitting, the divine way that love streams from heaven to earth: a spontaneous love flowing out to those who neither deserved it, bought it nor looked for it. It is, in fact, the only way God can love people like us. The text is a deathblow to every kind of fitness: “I will love them *freely*.” Now, if any fitness were needed in us, then he wouldn’t love us freely; at least, it would reduce and take away from the freeness of it. But it stands: “I will love you freely.”

We complain, “Lord, my heart is so hard.” “I will love you *freely*.” “But I don’t feel my need of Christ as I’d like to.” “I won’t love you because you feel your need; I will love you freely.” “But I don’t feel the softening of spirit I could wish for.” Remember, softening of spirit isn’t a condition, for there are no conditions; the covenant of grace has no conditions at all. So we, without any fitness, may venture on the promise God made to us in Christ Jesus when he said, “He that believeth on him is not condemned.” It is blessed to know that God’s grace is free to us at all times, without preparation, without fitness, without money and without price! “I will love them freely.”

These words *invite backsliders to return*; in fact, the text was written especially for them: “I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely.” Backslider, surely the generosity of the promise will break your heart at once, and you’ll come back and seek the face of the Father you have wronged.
