modern:
There are times when all the promises and teachings of the Bible are no help at all unless a gracious hand applies them to us. We are thirsty, but too faint to crawl to the brook. When a soldier is wounded in battle, it’s little use for him to know that there are people at the hospital who can bind up his wounds, and medicines there to ease all the pain he is suffering: what he needs is to be carried there and to have the remedies applied. It’s the same with our souls, and to meet this need there is one, the Spirit of truth, who takes the things of Jesus and applies them to us. Don’t think Christ has put his joys on heavenly shelves for us to climb up to by ourselves. No, he comes near and pours his peace into our hearts. Christian, if you are struggling under deep distress tonight, your Father doesn’t give you promises and then leave you to draw them up from the Word like buckets from a well; the promises he has written in the Word he will write again on your heart. He will show you his love, and by his blessed Spirit he will drive away your cares and troubles.

Let it be known to you, mourner, that it is God’s own right to wipe every tear from his people’s eyes. The good Samaritan didn’t say, “Here is the wine, and here is the oil for you”; he actually poured in the oil and the wine. In the same way, Jesus not only gives you the sweet wine of the promise, but holds the golden cup to your lips and pours the lifeblood into your mouth. The poor, sick, travel-worn pilgrim isn’t merely strengthened to walk; he is carried on eagles’ wings. Glorious gospel, which provides everything for the helpless, which comes near to us when we can’t reach out for it, and brings us grace before we look for grace! There is as much glory in the giving as in the gift. Happy are the people who have the Holy Spirit to bring Jesus to them.

modern:
Many have deserted Christ and walked with him no more; but what reason do *you* have *to make a change*? Has there been any reason for it in the *past*? Hasn’t Jesus proved himself all-sufficient? He appeals to you this morning: “Have I been a wilderness unto you?” When your soul has simply trusted Jesus, have you ever been put to shame? Haven’t you found your Lord, up to now, a compassionate and generous friend, and hasn’t simple faith in him given you all the peace your spirit could want? Can you even dream of a better friend than he has been to you? Then don’t swap the old and tried for the new and false.

As for *the present*, can that force you to leave Christ? When we are hard pressed by this world, or by the harsher trials inside the church, we find it a most blessed thing to rest our head on our Savior’s chest. This is our joy today: that we are saved in him. And if this joy satisfies, why should we think of changing? Who trades gold for trash? We won’t give up the sun until we find a better light, nor leave our Lord until a brighter lover appears; and since this can never be, we’ll hold him with an undying grip and bind his name like a seal on our arm.

As for *the future*, can you think of anything that could happen that would make it necessary for you to mutiny, or desert the old flag to serve under another captain? We don’t think so. If life is long, he doesn’t change. If we are poor, what could be better than having Christ, who can make us rich? When we are sick, what more do we want than Jesus to make our bed in our sickness? When we die, isn’t it written that “neither death, nor life, nor things present, nor things to come, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord!” We say with Peter, “Lord, to whom shall we go?”

modern:
When is a Christian most likely to fall asleep? Isn’t it *when his circumstances in this life are prosperous*? Haven’t you found it so? When you had daily troubles to take to the throne of grace, weren’t you more wakeful than you are now? Easy roads make sleepy travelers. Another dangerous time is *when everything is going pleasantly in spiritual things*. Christian didn’t fall asleep when lions were in the way, or when he was wading through the river, or when he was fighting Apollyon; but when he had climbed halfway up the Hill Difficulty and came to a delightful shelter, he sat down and promptly fell asleep, to his great sorrow and loss. The Enchanted Ground is a place of soothing breezes, full of sweet scents and soft influences, all of which tend to lull pilgrims to sleep. Remember Bunyan’s description: “Then they came to an arbour, warm, and promising much refreshing to the weary pilgrims; for it was finely wrought above head, beautified with greens, and furnished with benches and settles. It had also in it a soft couch, where the weary might lean.” “The arbour was called the Slothful’s Friend, and was made on purpose to allure, if it might be, some of the pilgrims to take up their rest there when weary.”

You can be sure that it’s in easy places that people shut their eyes and wander into the dreamy land of forgetfulness. Old Erskine wisely remarked, “I like a roaring devil better than a sleeping devil.” No temptation is half as dangerous as not being tempted. The distressed soul doesn’t sleep; it’s after we come into peaceful confidence and full assurance that we are in danger of dozing off. The disciples fell asleep after they had seen Jesus transfigured on the mountaintop. Be careful, joyful Christian: good moods are close neighbors to temptations. Be as happy as you like, only be watchful.

modern:
Without sap a tree can’t flourish or even exist. *Vitality* is essential to a Christian. There must be *life*, a living principle put into us by God the Holy Spirit, or we can’t be trees of the Lord. The mere name of Christian is a dead thing; we must be filled with the spirit of divine life. This life is *mysterious*. We don’t understand how sap circulates, by what force it rises and by what power it comes down again. In the same way, the life inside us is a sacred mystery. New birth is worked by the Holy Spirit entering a person and becoming that person’s life; and afterward this divine life in a believer feeds on the flesh and blood of Christ and is kept going by that divine food. But where it comes from and where it goes, who can explain to us?

What a *secret* thing sap is! The roots go searching through the soil with their tiny spongy tips, but we can’t see them draw out the various gases or turn mineral into plant; this work is done down in the dark. Our root is Christ Jesus, and our life is hidden in him; this is the secret of the Lord. The root of the Christian life is as secret as the life itself. How *constantly active* the sap in the cedar is! In the Christian, the divine life is always full of energy: not always in bearing fruit, but in its inward workings. The believer’s *graces* aren’t every one of them in constant motion, but his life never stops beating inside him. He isn’t always working for God, but his heart is always living on him. As sap *shows itself in producing the leaves and fruit of the tree*, so in a truly healthy Christian, grace shows outwardly in his life and conversation. If you talk with him, he can’t help speaking about Jesus. If you notice his actions, you’ll see that he has been with Jesus. He has so much sap inside that it must fill his conduct and conversation with life.

modern:
The Lord Jesus loves his people so much that every day he is still doing a great deal for them that is like washing their dirty feet. He accepts their poorest actions; he feels their deepest sorrow; he hears their slightest wish; and he forgives their every sin. He is still their servant as well as their Friend and Master. He not only does majestic deeds for them, wearing the miter on his head and the precious jewels glittering on his breastplate, and standing up to plead for them, but humbly and patiently he still goes about among his people with the basin and the towel. He does this when he puts away from us, day by day, our constant weaknesses and sins.

Last night, when you knelt, you sadly confessed that much of your conduct wasn’t worthy of what you profess; and even tonight you must mourn again that you have fallen back into the very same folly and sin that special grace rescued you from long ago. And yet Jesus will be very patient with you. He will hear your confession of sin; he will say, “I will, be thou clean”; he will again apply the sprinkled blood, speak peace to your conscience and remove every spot. It is a great act of eternal love when Christ once for all pardons the sinner and puts him into the family of God; but what condescending patience there is when the Savior, with much long-suffering, bears with the repeated follies of his wayward disciple, day by day and hour by hour washing away the many sins of his erring but still dearly loved child! To dry up a flood of rebellion is something marvelous, but to put up with the constant dripping of repeated offenses, to bear with a never-ending trial of patience: this is divine indeed! While we find comfort and peace in our Lord’s daily cleansing, its right effect on us will be to make us more watchful and sharpen our desire for holiness. *Is it so*?

modern: Once the truth of God has gotten into the human heart and brought the whole person under its rule, no power on earth or in hell can drive it out. We don’t entertain it as a guest, but as the master of the house. This is a *Christian necessity*: no one is a Christian who doesn’t believe like this. Those who feel the living power of the gospel, and know the might of the Holy Spirit as he opens, applies and seals the Lord’s Word, would sooner be torn to pieces than be torn away from the gospel of their salvation. What a thousand mercies are wrapped up in the assurance that the truth will be with us forever: our living support, our dying comfort, our rising song, our eternal glory! This is *Christian privilege*; without it our faith would be worth little. Some truths we outgrow and leave behind, for they are only basics and lessons for beginners; but we can’t treat God’s truth that way, for though it is sweet food for babies, it is in the highest sense solid food for adults. The truth that we are sinners stays painfully with us, to humble us and make us watchful; the more blessed truth that whoever believes in the Lord Jesus will be saved stays with us as our hope and joy. Experience, far from loosening our hold on the doctrines of grace, has bound us to them more and more firmly. Our grounds and reasons for believing are now stronger and more numerous than ever, and we have reason to expect it will stay that way until in death we clasp the Savior in our arms.

Wherever this lasting love of the truth can be found, we are bound to show our love. No narrow circle can contain our gracious sympathies; our fellowship of heart must be as wide as the election of grace. A good deal of error may be mixed in with the truth someone has received; let’s fight the error but still love the brother for the measure of truth we see in him. Above all, let’s love and spread the truth ourselves.

modern: Her *hap was*: it just so happened. Yes, it seemed nothing but an accident, but how wonderfully God was directing it! Ruth had gone out with her mother-in-law’s blessing, under the care of her mother-in-law’s God, to humble but honorable work, and God’s providence was guiding every step. Little did she know that among the sheaves she would find a husband, that he would make her joint owner of all those broad acres, and that she, a poor foreigner, would become one of the ancestors of the great Messiah. God is very good to those who trust in him, and often surprises them with unexpected blessings. We have little idea what may happen to us tomorrow, but this sweet fact may cheer us: no good thing will be withheld. Chance is banished from the faith of Christians, for they see the hand of God in everything. The trivial events of today or tomorrow may have consequences of the highest importance. Lord, deal as graciously with your servants as you did with Ruth.

How blessed it would be if, wandering in the field of meditation tonight, we should happen on the place where our next Kinsman will show himself to us! Spirit of God, guide us to him. We would rather glean in his field than carry off the whole harvest from any other. Oh, for the footprints of his flock, which may lead us to the green pastures where he lives! This is a weary world when Jesus is away. We could do better without sun and moon than without him; but how divinely beautiful everything becomes in the glory of his presence! Our souls know the power that lives in Jesus, and can never be content without him. We’ll wait in prayer tonight until we happen on a part of the field that belongs to Jesus, where he will show himself to us.

modern:
Stingy souls skimp on what they give to the ministry and to missions, and call it good economy. Little do they dream that they are making themselves poorer by it. Their excuse is that they must look after their own families, and they forget that neglecting God’s house is the sure way to bring ruin on their own houses. Our God has a way in his providence by which he can make our efforts succeed beyond what we expected, or can defeat our plans to our confusion and dismay. By a turn of his hand he can steer our ship into a profitable channel, or run it aground in poverty and bankruptcy. Scripture teaches that the Lord makes the generous rich, and leaves the miserly to find out that holding back leads to poverty.

Over a very wide field of observation, I have noticed that the most generous Christians I know have always been the happiest, and almost without exception the most prosperous. I have seen the generous giver rise to wealth he never dreamed of; and I have just as often seen the mean, ungenerous miser sink into poverty through the very stinginess by which he thought he would rise. People trust good stewards with larger and larger sums, and it’s often the same with the Lord: he gives by cartloads to those who give by bushels. Where he doesn’t give wealth, the Lord makes the little into much through the contentment a sanctified heart feels in a portion whose tenth has been given to the Lord. Selfishness looks first to its own home, but godliness seeks first the kingdom of God and his righteousness; and in the long run selfishness is loss, and godliness is great gain. It takes faith to deal with our God with an open hand, but surely he deserves it from us; and all we can do is a very poor acknowledgment of how amazingly we are indebted to his goodness.

modern:
Everything under the moon is on the move; time knows nothing of rest. The solid earth is a rolling ball, and the great sun itself is a star obediently running its course around some greater light. Tides move the sea, winds stir the ocean of air, friction wears down the rock: change and death rule everywhere. The sea isn’t a miser’s storehouse for a fortune in water, for just as one force makes the waters flow into it, another lifts them out of it. People are born only to die; everything is hurry, worry and vexation of spirit. Friend of the unchanging Jesus, what a joy it is to think about your unchanging inheritance: your sea of bliss, which will always be full, since God himself will pour eternal rivers of pleasure into it. We are looking for a lasting city beyond the skies, and we won’t be disappointed.

This passage may well teach us gratitude. Father Ocean is a great receiver, but he is a generous giver too. What the rivers bring him he returns to the earth as clouds and rain. The person who takes everything and gives nothing back is out of step with the universe. To give to others is only sowing seed for ourselves. Whoever is a good enough steward to be willing to use his possessions for his Lord will be trusted with more. Friend of Jesus, are you giving back to him in line with the benefits you’ve received? Much has been given to you; what is your fruit? Have you done all you can? Can’t you do more? To be selfish is to be wicked. Suppose the ocean gave up none of its watery treasure: it would bring ruin on our race. God forbid that any of us should follow the ungenerous and destructive policy of living for ourselves. Jesus didn’t please himself. All fullness lives in him, but from his fullness we have all received. Oh, for the spirit of Jesus, so that from now on we may live not for ourselves!

modern:
Paul has four of these “*faithful sayings*.” The first is in [[1Tim.1.15|1 Timothy 1:15]]: “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.” The next is in [[1Tim.4.6|1 Timothy 4:6]]: “Godliness is profitable unto all things, having the promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come. This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation.” The third is in [[2Tim.2.12|2 Timothy 2:12]]: “It is a faithful saying—If we suffer with him we shall also reign with him”; and the fourth is in [[Titus.3.3|Titus 3:3]]: “This is a faithful saying, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works.”

We can trace a connection between these faithful sayings. The first lays the foundation of our eternal salvation in God’s free grace, as shown to us in the mission of the great Redeemer. The next affirms the double blessing we receive through this salvation, the blessings of the upper and lower springs, of time and of eternity. The third shows one of the duties the chosen people are called to: we are appointed to suffer for Christ, with the promise that “if we suffer, we shall also reign with him.” The last sets out the active side of Christian service, telling us to keep up good works diligently. So we have the root of salvation in free grace; next, the privileges of that salvation in the life that now is and in the life to come; and we also have the two great branches of suffering with Christ and serving with Christ, loaded with the fruits of the Spirit.

Treasure these faithful sayings. Let them be the guides of our life, our comfort and our instruction. The apostle to the Gentiles proved them faithful; they are faithful still, and not one word will fall to the ground. They are worthy of all acceptance; let’s accept them now and prove their faithfulness. Let these four faithful sayings be written on the four corners of my house.

notes.note: Spurgeon’s verse numbers are a little off: these sayings are at [[1Tim.4.8-1Tim.4.9|1 Timothy 4:8–9]], [[2Tim.2.11-2Tim.2.12|2 Timothy 2:11–12]] and [[Titus.3.8|Titus 3:8]]. He also quotes from memory; Paul writes, “If we suffer, we shall also reign with him.”

modern:
The believer is a new creation. He belongs to a holy generation and a special people; the Spirit of God is in him, and in every way he is far removed from the natural man. But for all that, the Christian is still a sinner. He is one because his nature is imperfect, and he will stay one to the end of his earthly life. The black fingers of sin leave smudges on our finest robes. Sin spoils our repentance before the great Potter has finished it on the wheel. Selfishness stains our tears, and unbelief tampers with our faith. The best thing we ever did, apart from the merit of Jesus, only added to the number of our sins; for when we have been purest in our own sight, we are still, like the heavens, not pure in God’s sight; and since he charged his angels with folly, he must charge us with it much more, even in our most angelic moods.

The song that thrills up to heaven and tries to match the music of the seraphim has human discords in it. The prayer that moves the arm of God is still a bruised and battered prayer, and moves that arm only because the sinless One, the great Mediator, has stepped in to take away the sin of our asking. The most golden faith, or the purest holiness a Christian ever reached on earth, still has so much impurity in it that, taken by itself, it deserves only the flames. Every night we look in the mirror we see a sinner, and we need to confess, “We are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.”

Oh, how precious the blood of Christ is to hearts like ours! What a priceless gift his perfect righteousness is! And how bright the hope of perfect holiness hereafter! Even now, though sin lives in us, *its power is broken*. It has no rule over us; it is a snake with a broken back. We are in bitter conflict with it, but the enemy we have to deal with is a defeated one. Just a little while, and we’ll enter in victory into the city where nothing defiles.

modern: Here is distinguishing grace and discriminating regard, for some are made the special objects of God’s love. Don’t be afraid to dwell on this high doctrine of election. When your mind is heaviest and most depressed, you’ll find it a bottle of the richest tonic. Those who doubt the doctrines of grace, or push them into the shadows, miss the richest clusters of Eshcol; they lose the aged wines, well refined, the rich food full of marrow. There is no balm in Gilead to compare with it. If the honey in Jonathan’s wood brightened *the eyes* when he only touched it, this is honey that will enlighten *your heart* to love and learn the mysteries of the kingdom of God. Eat, and don’t fear eating too much; live on this choice delicacy, and don’t fear it will be too rich a diet. Food from the King’s table won’t hurt any of his courtiers. Long for your mind to be enlarged, so that you may grasp more and more the eternal, everlasting, discriminating love of God. When you have climbed as high as election, linger on its sister mountain, the covenant of grace. Covenant promises are the defenses of massive rock behind which we lie entrenched; covenant promises made with our guarantor, Christ Jesus, are the quiet resting places of trembling spirits.

If Jesus undertook to bring me to glory, and if the Father promised to give me to the Son as part of the infinite reward for the agony of his soul, then, my soul, until God himself becomes unfaithful, until Jesus stops being the truth, you are safe. When David danced before the ark, he told Michal that election made him do it. Come, my soul, rejoice before the God of grace, and leap for joy of heart.

modern: All comparisons fail to describe the Lord Jesus, but the bride uses the best within her reach. By *the head* of Jesus we may understand his deity, “for the head of Christ is God”; and then the ingot of purest gold is the best picture we could imagine, yet far too poor to describe someone so precious, so pure, so dear, so glorious. Jesus isn’t a grain of gold but a vast globe of it, a priceless mass of treasure such as earth and heaven can’t surpass. Created things are mere iron and clay; they will all perish like wood, hay and stubble; but the ever-living Head of God’s creation will shine on forever and ever. In him is no mixture, not the smallest trace of impurity. He is forever infinitely holy and altogether divine. *The bushy locks* show his manly strength. There is nothing effeminate about our Beloved. He is the manliest of men: bold as a lion, hardworking as an ox, swift as an eagle. Every beauty we can imagine, and every one we can’t, is found in him, though he was once despised and rejected by men.

The glory of his head isn’t shorn away; he is crowned forever with matchless majesty. *The black hair* shows youthful freshness, for Jesus has the dew of his youth on him. Others grow weary with age, but he is a Priest forever, like Melchizedek; others come and go, but he remains as God on his throne, world without end. We will look at him tonight and adore him. Angels are gazing at him; his redeemed mustn’t turn their eyes away from him. Where else is there anyone like our Beloved? Oh, for an hour’s fellowship with him! Away, you intruding cares! Jesus draws me, and I run after him.

modern: This prayer begins where all true prayer must begin, with the spirit of *adoption*: “Our Father.” There is no acceptable prayer until we can say, “I will arise, and go unto my Father.” This childlike spirit soon sees the greatness of the Father “in heaven,” and rises to *devout worship*: “Hallowed be thy name.” The child lisping “Abba, Father” grows into the cherub crying “Holy, Holy, Holy.” It’s only a step from rapturous worship to the *glowing missionary spirit*, which surely grows out of a child’s love and reverent worship: “Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” Next comes the heartfelt *expression of dependence* on God: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Further enlightened by the Spirit, the one praying discovers that he is not only dependent but sinful, so he *pleads for mercy*: “Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors.” And once pardoned, with the righteousness of Christ credited to him and knowing he is accepted by God, he humbly *asks for holy perseverance*: “Lead us not into temptation.” Someone who is really forgiven is anxious not to offend again; having justification leads to an anxious desire for sanctification. “Forgive us our debts”: that is justification. “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil”: that is sanctification, in its negative and positive forms. As the result of all this comes a *triumphant ascription of praise*: “Thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory, for ever and ever, Amen.” We rejoice that *our* King reigns in providence and will reign in grace, from the river to the ends of the earth, and of his rule there will be no end. So this short model of prayer leads the soul from a sense of adoption up to fellowship with our reigning Lord. Lord, teach us to pray like this.

modern:
The disciples ought to have known Jesus. They had heard his voice so often and looked at that marred face so many times that it’s amazing they didn’t recognize him. Yet isn’t it the same with you? You haven’t seen Jesus lately. You have been to his table, and you haven’t met him there. You are in dark trouble this evening, and though he plainly says, “It is I, be not afraid,” you can’t make him out. Sadly, our eyes are held. We know his voice; we have looked into his face; we have leaned our head on his chest; and yet, though Christ is very near us, we are saying, “O that I knew where I might find him!” We should know Jesus, for we have the Scriptures to reflect his image; and yet how possible it is for us to open that precious book and catch no glimpse of the Well-beloved! Dear child of God, are you in that state? Jesus feeds among the lilies of the Word, and you walk among those lilies, and yet you don’t see him. He is used to walking through the glades of Scripture and talking with his people, as the Father did with Adam in the cool of the day; yet you are in the garden of Scripture and can’t see him, though he is always there.

And why don’t we see him? In our case, as in the disciples’, it must be put down to unbelief. They clearly didn’t expect to see Jesus, and so they didn’t recognize him. To a great extent in spiritual things, we get what we expect from the Lord. Only faith can bring us to see Jesus. Make this your prayer: “Lord, open my eyes, so that I may see my Savior present with me.” It is a blessed thing to want to see him; but oh, it is far better to gaze on him! To those who seek him he is kind; but to those who find him, he is dear beyond words!

modern:
Praise should always follow answered prayer, as the mist of earth’s gratitude rises when the sun of heaven’s love warms the ground. Has the Lord been gracious to you, and turned his ear to the voice of your prayer? Then praise him as long as you live. Let the ripe fruit drop onto the fertile soil it drew its life from. Don’t deny a song to the one who has answered your prayer and given you your heart’s desire. To keep silent about God’s mercies is to be guilty of ingratitude; it’s to act as shabbily as the nine lepers who, after they were cured of their leprosy, didn’t come back to thank the Lord who healed them. To forget to praise God is to refuse to do ourselves good; for praise, like prayer, is one of the great means of promoting the growth of the spiritual life. It helps to lift our burdens, to stir up our hope, to increase our faith. It is a healthy, invigorating exercise that quickens the believer’s pulse and braces him for new undertakings in his Master’s service.

Blessing God for the mercies we have received is also the way to do good to others: “the humble shall hear thereof and be glad.” Others who have been in the same circumstances will take comfort if we can say, “Oh! magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together; this poor man cried, and the Lord heard him.” Weak hearts will be strengthened, and drooping saints revived, as they listen to our “songs of deliverance.” Their doubts and fears will be rebuked as we teach and encourage one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. They too will “sing in the ways of the Lord” when they hear us magnify his holy name. Praise is the most heavenly of Christian duties. The angels don’t pray, but they never stop praising, day and night; and the redeemed, clothed in white robes with palm branches in their hands, never tire of singing the new song: “Worthy is the Lamb.”

modern:
My sweet Lord Jesus remembers the garden of Gethsemane well, and although he has left that garden, he now lives in the garden of his church. There he opens his heart to those who keep his blessed company. That voice of love with which he speaks to his beloved is more musical than the harps of heaven. There is a depth of melodious love in it that leaves all human music far behind. Tens of thousands on earth, and millions above, are treated to its harmonious tones. Some whom I know well, and greatly envy, are listening to that dear voice right now. Oh, that I shared their joys! It’s true that some of them are poor, others bedridden, and some near the gates of death; but, my Lord, I would cheerfully starve with them, waste away with them or die with them, if only I might hear your voice.

I used to hear it often, but I have grieved your Spirit. Come back to me in compassion, and say to me once again, “I am thy salvation.” No other voice can content me. I know your voice, and can’t be fooled by another; let me hear it, I beg you. I don’t know what you will say, and I make no conditions, my Beloved; only let me hear you speak, and if it is a rebuke, I’ll bless you for it. Perhaps cleansing my dull ear will take an operation very painful to the flesh; but whatever it costs, I won’t turn from this one consuming desire: let me hear your voice. Bore my ear again; pierce my ear with your harshest notes; only don’t let me stay deaf to your calls. Tonight, Lord, grant your unworthy one his desire, for I am yours, and you have bought me with your blood. You have opened my eye to see you, and the sight has saved me. Lord, open my ear. I have read your heart; now let me hear your lips.

modern:
A backslider, if there is a spark of life left in him, will groan to be restored. This renewal needs the same work of grace as our conversion. We needed repentance then; we certainly need it now. We needed faith to come to Christ at first; only the same grace can bring us to Jesus now. We needed a word from the Most High, a word from the lips of the loving One, to end our fears then; we’ll soon find out, when we feel our present sin, that we need it now. No one can be renewed without as real and true a display of the Holy Spirit’s power as he felt at first, because the work is just as great, and flesh and blood are as much in the way now as they ever were.

Christian, let your own weakness be a reason to pray earnestly to your God for help. Remember, when David felt powerless, he didn’t fold his arms or close his lips, but hurried to the mercy-seat with “renew a right spirit within me.” Don’t let the teaching that on your own you can do nothing make you sleep; let it be a goad in your side, driving you with awed earnestness to Israel’s strong Helper. Oh, may you have grace to plead with God as though you were pleading for your very life: “Lord, renew a right spirit within me.”

Whoever *sincerely* prays for God to do this will prove his honesty by using the means God works through. Pray much; live much on the Word of God; kill the desires that have driven your Lord away from you; watch carefully for sin rising up again in the future. The Lord has his own appointed ways; sit by the roadside, and you’ll be ready when he passes by. Keep on in all those blessed ordinances that will feed and nourish your dying graces; and, knowing that all the power must come from him, never stop crying, “Renew a right spirit within me.”

modern: Yes, Lord, you did indeed know me in my *fallen state*, and even then you chose me for yourself. When I was loathsome and loathed myself, you received me as your child and satisfied my desperate needs. Blessed forever be your name for this free, rich, overflowing mercy. Since then, my *inner experience* has often been a wilderness; but you have still claimed me as your beloved, and poured streams of love and grace into me to gladden me and make me fruitful. Yes, when my *outward circumstances* have been at their worst, and I have wandered in a land of drought, your sweet presence has comforted me. People haven’t known me when scorn was waiting for me, but you have known my soul in adversities, for no trouble dims the luster of your love. Most gracious Lord, I praise you for all your faithfulness to me in hard times, and I grieve that I should ever have forgotten you and grown proud in heart, when I have owed everything to your gentleness and love. Have mercy on your servant in this!

My soul, if Jesus acknowledged you like this in your low state, make sure you own both him and his cause now that you are prospering. Don’t be so puffed up by your worldly success that you are ashamed of the truth, or of the poor church you have belonged to. Follow Jesus into the wilderness; carry the cross with him when the heat of persecution grows hot. He owned you, my soul, in your poverty and shame; never be so treacherous as to be ashamed of him. Oh, for more shame at the very thought of being ashamed of the Beloved of my soul! Jesus, my soul clings to you.
